job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

passage: Teacher: Today, let us clarify some common doubts about carbon compounds. Rohan, remember that carbon’s versatility comes from its ability to form stable covalent bonds, not just single ones; it can form double or triple bonds too. Priya: Sir, does that mean covalent bonds are weaker than ionic ones? Teacher: Not at all. Covalent bonds are strong because they involve shared electron pairs, not just a temporary association. Rohan: What about alcohols like ethanol? Since they have an -OH group, are they basic like sodium hydroxide? Teacher: That is a common mistake. Ethanol is neutral because the -OH group is covalently bonded to a carbon chain, not an ionizable hydroxide group. Priya: I see. And what about homologous series? Do all members have identical physical properties? Teacher: No, while they share similar chemical properties, their physical properties like boiling point change as the molecular mass increases. Finally, remember that soap molecules are not flat circles; they form three-dimensional spherical structures called micelles in water. The hydrophobic tail is actually water-repelling, which is why it attaches to oil, not water. This structure is essential for cleaning.

items.evidence: Ethanol is neutral because the -OH group is covalently bonded to a carbon chain, not an ionizable hydroxide group.
items.q: Why does ethanol not behave like sodium hydroxide in water?
options: Its carbon chain makes it a base
Its -OH is weaker than in NaOH
items.explain: The -OH in ethanol is covalently bonded to the carbon chain, so it is not ionizable and ethanol stays neutral.

wrong.why: thinks the -OH group always makes a solution basic
reverses the cause: thinks the carbon chain gives basic nature
thinks covalent bonds are weaker than ionic ones

items.evidence: Covalent bonds are strong because they involve shared electron pairs, not just a temporary association.
items.q: Priya thinks sharing electrons is less permanent than giving them away. What corrects her?
options: Shared electron pairs hold atoms firmly
Shared electrons are held by one atom only
Giving electrons makes bonds last longer
Sharing happens only for a short time
items.explain: Covalent bonds are strong because they involve shared electron pairs, not a temporary association.

wrong.why: thinks shared electrons belong only to the atom that brought them
repeats the belief that giving is more permanent than sharing
turns 'temporary association' into a description of covalent bonds

items.evidence: No, while they share similar chemical properties, their physical properties like boiling point change as the molecular mass increases.
items.q: Two members of a homologous series differ in molecular mass. How will their boiling points compare?
options: They will differ, as mass changes boiling point
They will match, as chemistry is similar
They will match, as the group is the same
They will differ, as chemistry changes with mass
items.explain: Members share chemical properties, but physical properties like boiling point change as molecular mass increases.

wrong.why: thinks members have identical physical properties
thinks same functional group means same physical properties
mixes up which properties change with mass

items.evidence: The hydrophobic tail is actually water-repelling, which is why it attaches to oil, not water.
items.q: How does a soap molecule help remove oil from a cloth?
options: Its tail sticks to the oil
Its tail pulls in the water
Its tail dissolves in the water
Its tail forms a flat circle
items.explain: The hydrophobic tail repels water, so it attaches to oil and helps lift it away.

wrong.why: thinks the hydrophobic tail attracts water
confuses the tail with the water-loving head
